chapters.title: Chapter 1 · The Silver Saucer and the Transparent Apple
chapters.artPrompt: a Russian village girl spinning a transparent glassy apple in a silver dish on a wooden table by a warm tiled stove, swirling silver mist inside the dish showing tiny ships and golden domes, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Long ago a rich merchant lived in a wooden hut with his three daughters. The two elder girls loved looking-glasses and new dresses. They called the youngest "Little Stupid", because she was so good and did all the work. One year the merchant set out for the great fair of Nijni Novgorod. "What shall I bring you, little pigeons?" he asked. The eldest asked for a rich necklace. The second asked for a dress with gold hems. The youngest asked for a silver saucer and a transparent apple. "I shall spin the apple in the saucer," she said softly.

At home the good sister cooked and swept while the others strutted in their finery. She set the clear apple in the silver dish and spun it round. Round and round it spun, faster and faster, like a little whirlpool of mist. "Spin, spin, apple," she whispered. "Let me see the wide world." And she saw it all in the shining mist. The Tzar on his high throne. Ships with white sails on the blue sea. Painted churches, and the great river Volga flowing to the sea. Her sisters looked over her shoulder, and envy filled their hard hearts.

New word: transparent — clear like glass, so that you can see right through it. A transparent apple shines like a round little window. If you spin it in a silver saucer, the old tale says, you may see far-away towns and rivers in the mist.

The sisters begged her to trade, but she would not give up her treasure. So they made a cruel plan. They took their father's axe and hid it under a bush in the deep forest. Next day they asked her to come and gather berries. Among the trees they turned on her with hard eyes and empty baskets. "Give us the saucer and the apple," they said. "I have left them safe at home," she answered. Then the wicked sisters killed the little good one, and buried her under a birch tree. They went home crying false tears about wolves.
The little good sister spins the transparent apple in the silver saucer and sees the wide world in the mist.

When the snow melted, a young shepherd followed lost lambs into the forest. Under a birch tree he found a flowery mound, and in it a single reed. He cut the reed and carved it into a whistle-pipe. Before his lips touched it, the pipe began to play by itself. "Play, play, whistle-pipe!" it sang. "I was killed for the sake of a silver saucer." The old merchant heard the song, and his tears ran into his beard. They dug beneath the birch tree and found the girl lying as if asleep. The whistle sang again: "Fetch water from the well of the Tzar."

The Tzar gave water from his holy well, and the good sister opened her eyes. She leapt up, laughing and crying, and clung to her father's neck. The Tzar would have punished the sisters, but she fell on her knees. "Forgive them, little father," she begged. "Do not kill them because of me." The Tzar was pleased with her kind heart and forgave them all. Then he asked her to be his Tzaritza, and there was a grand wedding. The shepherd boy turned sadly away into the forest. But her father and mother came to live in the palace with her. "Let all be forgotten and all be forgiven," she said to her sisters.

New word: Tzar — the mighty emperor who ruled old Russia long ago. People called him the little father, and his wife the Tzaritza. A palace wedding for a Tzar was the grandest feast in the land, and every city sent gifts of bread and salt.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 · Frost
chapters.artPrompt: a little girl in a blue dress sitting under a huge snow-covered fir tree in a dark winter forest, frost sparkling and crackling on the branches above her, falling snow, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Once there was a little girl named Martha, whose own mother had died. Her father married again, and the new wife brought two daughters of her own. They gave their own girls jelly and honey, and left Martha only the scraps. Martha fetched wood, lit the stove, drew water, and cooked, and never once complained. Still the stepmother scolded her from morning till night. "There is dust on the floor," she would cry. "The spoons are not clean."

One winter the stepmother thought of a cruel trick. "Martha is to be married," she said. "Drive her to my chosen bridegroom, away in the forest." Martha packed her little box and put on her best blue dress, hoping and fearing. The old man drove the sledge deep into the snowy wood. At a great fir tree he set her down. "Wait here for your bridegroom," he said, "and greet him with kind words." Then he drove home, weeping, and the tears froze on his cheeks. Cold, cold it was, and Martha sat shivering under the fir.

New word: sledge — a light sleigh that slides over the snow, pulled by a horse. In the long Russian winters, when the roads were deep with snow, the sledge was the quickest and best way to travel through the forest.

Suddenly she heard a crackling among the trees. It was Frost, leaping from fir to fir. "Are you warm, little maid?" he called down. Though she was nearly frozen, Martha answered gently. "Warm, warm, little Father Frost." Frost climbed lower and crackled louder, and asked her again. Again she whispered, "Warm, dear Frost, warm, little father." Then Frost was sorry for her. He leapt down with a scatter of frozen snow, wrapped her in rich furs, and covered her with warm blankets.
Martha sits under the great fir tree while Frost leans down from the crackling branches above.

In the morning her father found her alive and singing, with a box of splendid presents. The stepmother was wild with envy. "Drive my daughters to that bridegroom too," she cried. So the two girls were left under the same fir tree. But they had no kind words ready. When Frost asked, "Are you warm, maidens?", they screamed rude words at him. And Frost crackled and crackled, till the cross sisters sat frozen stiff. The old man brought them home through the snow. As for Martha, she married the kind young man of her dreams. Kind words had won kindness, and cross words had won cold.

Father Frost is the spirit of the winter cold in Russian tales. He crackles and leaps among the fir trees. People greet him politely, because the old stories teach that kind words win kindness, and cross words win cold treatment.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 · The Fool of the World and the Flying Ship
chapters.artPrompt: a small wooden ship with patchwork sails flying through the blue sky above a green Russian forest, a cheerful singing crew of odd folk aboard, waving, storybook illustration

blocks.text: There were once three sons. Two were clever, but the youngest was the Fool of the World, gentle as a lamb. The Tzar promised his daughter to anyone who could bring him a flying ship. The clever brothers set off in fine clothes, with rich food and bottles of drink. The Fool went too, with a bag of dry crusts and a flask of water. Soon he met an ancient old man with a bent back. "Sit and share what you have," said the old man. The Fool opened his bag and stared. The dry crusts had turned to fresh white rolls and tasty meats.

The old man taught him a secret. Strike the first big tree with a little hatchet, lie down on your back, and wait. When the Fool woke, a little ship stood ready, and it flew up over the treetops. "Give a lift to everyone you meet," the old man had said. So the Fool gathered a wonderful crew. A Listener with his ear pressed to the ground. A Swift-goer who hopped on one leg. A Far-shooter, a mighty Eater, and a great Drinker. And two more men, one with magic sticks and one with magic straw.

New word: moujik — a simple country farmer in old Russia. When the Tzar's servant peeped into the flying ship, he saw only moujiks in rough peasant clothes. Because they looked poor, the Tzar thought he could break his promise and set them hard tasks.

The Tzar saw only dirty peasants in the ship, and set them hard tasks. First he wanted water of life before his dinner ended. The Swift-goer fetched it, though the Listener heard him snoring under a windmill. The Far-shooter woke him with a shot, and the water arrived in time. Then came twelve roasted oxen and bread from forty ovens. The Eater ate the lot and called it a snack. Then forty barrels of wine. The Drinker drank them every one, and was thirsty still. Last of all the Tzar made an iron bath-house red hot. But the man with the magic straw made it so cold inside that the water froze.
The flying ship sails through the blue sky, crowded with the Fool's singing crew of queer companions.

In the night the man with the magic sticks walked about, scattering them on the ground. Where each stick fell, a soldier leapt up, with horses and guns and shining uniforms. In the morning the Tzar looked out at troops upon troops, and was afraid at last. He sent jewels and fine clothes, and begged the Fool to come to the palace. The Fool put them on, and stood there as handsome as any prince. He fell in love with the Princess, and she with him. They were married that very day, and the whole court sang their praises.

The Fool of the World wins every prize by being kind. He shares his last crust with a hungry old man, and he gives a lift to every stranger he meets. In Russian tales, a gentle heart often brings the greatest luck of all.

chapters.title: Chapter 4 · Baba Yaga
chapters.artPrompt: a little girl running down a moonlit forest path, behind her an old witch flying in a wooden mortar with a pestle, far back a crooked hut standing on chicken legs among fir trees, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Once there was a little girl with a kind heart. Her father married again, and the new wife was cross and cold. The stepmother said that everything that went wrong was the little girl's fault. She threw her a dry crust and sent her out of the hut to eat it. In the shed the girl made friends with a little gray mouse, and shared her crust with him. "Thank you," squeaked the mouse. "Beware, for the old woman is sister to Baba Yaga, the witch. If ever she sends you to your aunt, come and tell me."

Soon the stepmother sent her to the dear aunt in the forest, to ask for a needle and thread. The mouse crept along the road beside her. "Take every little thing you find," he said, "and you will escape from Baba Yaga." Her towel held nothing but stones, but the mouse turned them into bread and jam. On the way she picked up a handkerchief. Then a bottle of oil. Then scraps of meat, a blue ribbon, and a little loaf.

Baba Yaga is the witch of the old Russian tales. Her hut stands on chicken legs and walks about the yard. She flies through the sky in a big wooden mortar, driving it with a pestle, and she sweeps away her tracks with a besom.

At last she came to a fence with squeaking gates. Behind it stood a little hut on hen's legs, walking about the yard. How lucky she had picked up the oil! She poured it on the gates, and they swung open without a sound. A thin dog gnawed a dry crust, so she gave him the loaf. A crying servant wiped her eyes, so she gave her the handkerchief. Inside sat Baba Yaga at her loom, gnashing her iron teeth. "Sit and weave, niece," she smiled, "while I fetch your needle and thread." But she whispered to her servant, "Make the bath hot and scrub my niece. I'll make a dainty meal of her."

The girl gave her scraps of meat to the thin black cat. "I will help you," said the cat. "Take your towel and your comb, and run. When Baba Yaga is close, throw the towel. It will become a wide river. Then throw the comb. It will become a thick forest." The cat took her place at the loom, clickety clack, and tangled every thread. The girl ran. The dog let her pass. The gates were quiet. The birch tree stood still to admire its pretty blue ribbon.
The little girl runs down the road while Baba Yaga flies after her in the mortar.

Baba Yaga jumped into her mortar and drove it with a pestle, sweeping her tracks with a besom. Bang, bang, bangety bang! The girl heard her close behind and threw the towel. Up grew a deep, wide river. Baba Yaga made her cattle drink it dry, and flew on. Again the pestle banged, and the girl threw the comb. Up sprang a forest so thick that even Baba Yaga could not pass. So the witch turned home, raging and gnashing her teeth. The girl ran home to her father and told him everything. The old man drove the stepmother out of the hut for ever. And the little mouse came to live in the house, warming his paws on her glass of tea.

New word: besom — a broom made of bundled twigs. In the tale Baba Yaga sweeps her tracks away with a besom as she flies. A mortar is a strong bowl, and a pestle is the heavy stick used to pound things inside it.

chapters.title: Chapter 5 · The Cat Who Became Head-Forester
chapters.artPrompt: a shaggy one-eared cat standing fiercely over an ox in a forest clearing, a bear hiding high in a fir tree, a wolf hiding under dry leaves, a fox watching from behind a tree, storybook illustration

blocks.text: An old peasant had a tom-cat with only one ear, and he did not like him. He sewed the cat in a sack and threw it deep in the forest. But cats always fall on their feet. The tom-cat tore his way out, and washed his whiskers in the sunshine. "The world seems larger than the village," said he. "I will walk on and see what there is in it." He found an empty forester's hut, and made his bed in the hay.

Next day he met a pretty young fox, who had never seen such a strange beast. "I am Cat Ivanovitch," said the cat, swelling his fur. "I am sent from the far forests of Siberia to be Head-forester over you." The fox made her best bows at once. "Will your Excellency honour my house?" she asked. Her name was Lisabeta Ivanovna. They married, and ate up every dainty in her store.

New word: Head-forester — the chief keeper of a forest, whom every beast must obey. The clever cat gave himself this grand title, and the fox believed every word. Sometimes in tales a little swagger, kept up bravely, is enough to fool even a bear.

The fox told the wolf to bring a sheep as a greeting gift. She told the bear to bring an ox. "Hide yourselves well," she warned them. The bear climbed a tall fir. The wolf crouched under dry leaves, with only his nose showing. The cat tore at the ox, purring loudly. The bear thought the purring said, "Small, small, small." "What a glutton!" he whispered. "Heaven help us if he comes after us!" Then the leaves rustled, ever so little. The cat heard, and sprang with all four paws on the wolf's nose. How the wolf yelped and ran!
The one-eared tom-cat tears at the ox while the bear and the wolf hide from him.

The cat was frightened too, and leapt up the very tree where the bear was hiding. The bear jumped from the treetop, broke many branches, and stumbled away groaning. "Run, run!" cried the fox. "His Excellency is close behind!" From that day every beast in the forest feared the cat. The cat and the fox live merrily together still. Fresh meat is left for them a little way off, which other animals kill for them.

Siberia is a vast, cold part of Russia, covered with deep forests where few people live. A grand stranger from the far forests of Siberia sounded very important to the fox, so she bowed low and made her very best dinner.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 · The Little Daughter of the Snow
chapters.artPrompt: a magical snow girl with blue eyes and long black hair dancing in a moonlit village yard, snowflakes swirling around her, an old couple watching from a lit window of a wooden hut, storybook illustration

blocks.text: An old man and an old woman lived at the edge of the forest. They were happy in everything but one. They had no child of their own. All winter they watched the village children pelting snowballs and building snow witches. "Wife," said the old man, "let us make a little snow girl. Perhaps she will come alive." So they rolled the snow very tenderly, and made a little daughter with white eyes and closed lips. And she did come alive. Her eyes shone blue, her lips opened in a smile, and her black hair stirred in the wind. She danced in the snow like a little white spirit.

They wrapped her in a blanket, but she would not be kept warm. She ate porridge of crushed ice, and slept out in the yard all night. By day she played with the village children, and no one could run faster or throw truer snowballs. The old people were proud and happy. "She is all our own," said the old woman. All through the winter the little daughter of the Snow sang and laughed and danced.

New word: porridge — a soft, warm dish of boiled grain that children eat for breakfast. The little daughter of the Snow ate a different kind. Her porridge was made of crushed ice in a wooden bowl, and she liked it very much.

But when spring came, she went too far into the wood and lost her friends in the dusk. She climbed a tree and called for help. A brown bear offered to carry her home. "I am afraid you would eat me," she said. A gray wolf offered too, and she feared him also. Then a red fox came running on little pads. "I am not afraid of you," she said. So she held the fox by the hair of his back, and he brought her home safe.
The little daughter of the Snow dances in the moonlit yard, tossing her dark hair while the snow flies.

The fox asked a plump hen for his pay. The old woman put a hen in one sack and their fiercest dog in another. The fox got neither, for the dog leapt out with flashing eyes, and the fox fled to the deep forest. Then the little snow girl began to sing. "Old ones, old ones, now I know you love me less than a hen. I shall melt away again." They ran in and found a little pool of water, a fur hat, a coat, and red boots. She had leapt to Frost her father and Snow her mother, far over the stars. And in winter, when children build snow figures, sometimes she comes dancing back.

In this tale the snow girl's father is Frost and her mother is Snow. They carry her far over the stars to the north, where she plays on the frozen seas all summer. When winter comes again, she may dance back to Russia.
